title: Multiplexing
explain: Multiplexing means carrying several independent conversations over one shared channel and telling them apart again at the other end. I use it to avoid paying a connection per request: fewer handshakes, fewer ports, less memory. HTTP/2 and gRPC do it by putting many streams on one TCP connection.
model:
Two flavours, matching how you would say it:

1. **Share one channel.** Many senders use the same medium and something tells them apart. TCP does this on the host: every client hits the same `IP:port` and the kernel demultiplexes by the full 4-tuple (see [TCP connections](#/sd/f/tcp-connection)).
2. **Share one connection for arbitrary byte streams.** TCP is an undifferentiated byte stream, so the protocol on top adds **framing** (message boundaries) and a **stream ID** per frame.

```
one TCP connection
[hdr s1|data][hdr s3|data][hdr s2|data][hdr s1|data] ...   <- interleaved frames
```

HTTP/2 and gRPC work like this; hundreds of requests are in flight at once, capped by the server's advertised max concurrent streams.

**Costs:** TCP-level head-of-line blocking, uneven load balancing with connection-level balancers, and a single connection failure hurting every stream. HTTP/3 (QUIC) fixes the first. See [load balancing](#/sd/f/load-balancing).

details.q: What must a protocol add on top of TCP to multiplex requests?
details.a: Framing, so the receiver knows where each message ends, and a stream ID in each frame, so it knows which request a chunk belongs to. TCP itself gives only ordered bytes with no boundaries or tags.

details.q: How many connections does a client need for 500 concurrent requests if the server allows 100 streams per connection?
details.a: At least 5 (500 / 100). Over HTTP/1.1 without pipelining the same load needs about 500 connections, one per outstanding request.

details.q: What happens to 50 HTTP/2 streams when one packet is lost?
details.a: All 50 stall until TCP retransmits it, because TCP releases bytes strictly in order. This is TCP head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 over QUIC recovers loss per stream, so only the affected stream waits.

details.q: Why do newly added backends get almost no traffic from long-lived gRPC clients behind an L4 balancer?
details.a: An L4 balancer picks a backend once, at connect time, and each connection multiplexes all its requests to that backend. Fix by balancing per request at L7, balancing in the client, or having servers close connections periodically so clients reconnect.

details.q: What does multiplexing buy you for ports and handshakes?
details.a: Many requests reuse one connection, so you pay one TCP and one TLS handshake, consume one 4-tuple, hold one set of buffers, and keep a warmed-up congestion window. It is the core fix for ephemeral-port and connection exhaustion.

details.q: When is multiplexing a poor choice?
details.a: When a big transfer would starve small requests on the same connection, on lossy links where head-of-line blocking dominates, or when you rely on connection-level balancing for even spread. Then use several connections or HTTP/3.

prompts.q: Explain multiplexing and its two flavours.
points: Many conversations over one channel, separated at the receiver
Connection level: one connection, many streams
Framing and stream IDs are needed because TCP is a plain byte stream

prompts.q: Give the benefits and costs of putting many requests on one connection.
points: Fewer handshakes, ports and buffers; warm congestion window
One connection failure hits all streams

prompts.q: Your gRPC service scaled out from 3 to 6 backends but the new ones sit idle. Explain and fix.
points: L4 balancing decided only at connect time
Fix options: L7 per-request balancing, client-side balancing, periodic connection recycling
